report.source_text: The patient then underwent placement of a double-J stent with Foley catheter placement. The patient was discharged with oral antibiotics and outpatient follow-up for repeat cystoscopy and evaluation for possible stent removal in one month. The patient’s postoperative course was complicated by transient hematuria with outpatient CT urogram showing satisfactory positioning of the left ureteral stent without hydronephrosis, no contrast extravasation, and symmetric excretion of contrast material bilaterally. The patient ultimately underwent a repeat cystoscopy with left ureteroscopy and double-JJ stent removal with no noted stones, tumors within the ureter or within the renal pelvis, and no evidence of extravasation of the ureter.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 67-year-old female presented with acute severe left flank pain, nausea, and emesis. Initial CT revealed an edematous left kidney, dilated left collecting system, and moderate perinephric and periureteric fluid, notably without an obstructing calculus. A subsequent CT with delayed images (CT urogram) confirmed extravasation of contrast from the left proximal and mid-ureter. Cystoscopy and left-sided retrograde pyelogram further confirmed extravasation 2 cm distal to the left ureteropelvic junction and ruled out stones, filling defects, or other etiologies for the rupture. The patient was treated with intravenous antibiotics, fluids, and underwent placement of a double-J stent. Her postoperative course included transient hematuria, and a follow-up CT urogram showed satisfactory stent positioning with no hydronephrosis or contrast extravasation. Ultimately, the patient underwent repeat cystoscopy with left ureteroscopy and double-JJ stent removal, with no evidence of stones, tumors, or extravasation.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with acute onset of severe left flank pain, nausea, and multiple episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis.
Initial CT scan revealed an edematous left kidney with dilation of the left collecting system and moderate perinephric and periureteric fluid, without the presence of an obstructing calculus.
CT with delayed images (CT urogram) showed extravasation of contrast from the left proximal as well as mid-ureter.

Cystoscopy and left-sided retrograde pyelogram confirmed extravasation of contrast 2 cm distal to the left ureteropelvic junction and ruled out stones, filling defects, or other etiologies of the ureter rupture.
The patient underwent placement of a double-J stent, and follow-up imaging confirmed satisfactory stent positioning with no contrast extravasation, leading to successful stent removal.
